title: Νεῦσε Κρονίων
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Thetis clings to Zeus’ knees and asks for a plain yes or no. Vexed at the prospect of Hera’s abuse, he gives his binding nod, and Olympus shakes. As Thetis dives back into the sea and the gods rise to greet him, Hera, who has seen it all, taunts him for plotting in secret; he tells her to be silent and fear his hands, and she obeys. His son Hephaestus calms the gods: he hands his mother a cup, urges her to give way, and recalls how Zeus once flung him from Olympus to Lemnos. Hera smiles, Hephaestus pours the nectar, and the gods laugh as they watch him bustle. They feast until sunset to the lyre of Apollo and the song of the Muses, and then go to bed, Zeus beside Hera.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο· τὴν δ’ οὔ τι προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς,
ἀλλ’ ἀκέων δὴν ἧστο·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato· tēn d’ ou ti prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus,
all’ akeōn dēn hēsto·
sentences.l:
So she spoke; but her not at all addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus,
but in silence for a long time he sat;
sentences.i: So she spoke, but Zeus who gathers the clouds said nothing to her at all, and sat for a long time in silence;
sentences.n: Thetis has ended her plea (1.505–510), and Zeus does not answer. The subject of προσέφη is νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς, ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’, the old formula with the nominative in -α (Attic -ης); οὔ τι is ‘not at all’, so τὴν … οὔ τι προσέφη is ‘did not address her at all’. ἀκέων ‘in silence’ is a fixed adverbial form. ἧστο is the imperfect of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and δήν ‘for a long time’.

sentences.t:
Θέτις δ’ ὡς ἥψατο γούνων
ὣς ἔχετ’ ἐμπεφυυῖα, καὶ εἴρετο δεύτερον αὖτις·
sentences.tr:
Thetis d’ hōs hēpsato gounōn
hōs echet’ empephyuia, kai eireto deuteron autis·
sentences.l:
and Thetis, as she had touched his knees,
so held on, clinging to them, and asked a second time again:
sentences.i: and Thetis, just as she had laid hold of his knees, held on to them, clinging, and asked him a second time:
sentences.n: ὡς … ὣς is ‘just as … so’: she has not let go since she took hold of his knees at 500. ἥψατο is the aorist middle of ἅπτω ‘touch, lay hold of’, with the genitive γούνων ‘knees’. ἔχετ’ is the imperfect middle of ἔχω, ‘held on’, with ἐμπεφυυῖα, the feminine perfect participle of ἐμφύω ‘grow into’, hence ‘clinging’. εἴρετο is the aorist of εἴρομαι ‘ask’, and δεύτερον αὖτις ‘a second time again’ is a doubled phrase: this is her second request, after her long first speech.

sentences.t:
νημερτὲς μὲν δή μοι ὑπόσχεο καὶ κατάνευσον
ἢ ἀπόειπ’,
sentences.tr:
nēmertes men dē moi hyposcheo kai kataneuson
ē apoeip’,
sentences.l:
“Unerringly now promise me and nod assent,
or refuse,
sentences.i: “Promise me truly now, and nod your assent, or else refuse,
sentences.n: She asks for a plain yes or no. νημερτές ‘unerringly, without fail’ is a neuter adjective used as an adverb. ὑπόσχεο is the aorist imperative middle of ὑπίσχομαι ‘promise’, and κατάνευσον the aorist imperative of κατανεύω ‘nod assent’; the nod is Zeus’ sign of binding consent, and it is the gesture of 524 and 528. ἀπόειπ’ is the aorist imperative of ἀπεῖπον ‘say no, refuse’, its final -ε elided.

sentences.t:
ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι ἔπι δέος, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδέω
ὅσσον ἐγὼ μετὰ πᾶσιν ἀτιμοτάτη θεός εἰμι.
sentences.tr:
epei ou toi epi deos, ophr’ eÿ eideō
hosson egō meta pasin atimotatē theos eimi.
sentences.l:
since there is no fear upon you, so that I may know well
how far among all I am the most dishonoured goddess.”
sentences.i: since you have nothing to fear, so that I may know well how far I am the most dishonoured goddess among them all.”
sentences.n: ἔπι is ἔπεστι ‘is upon, is there’ with the accent thrown back, so οὔ τοι ἔπι δέος is ‘there is no fear upon you’; τοι is the enclitic ‘to you’. ἐῢ is the epic form of εὖ ‘well’, and εἰδέω the epic subjunctive of οἶδα, ‘I may know’, after ὄφρα. μετὰ πᾶσιν is ‘among all’ (the gods understood). ἀτιμοτάτη is the superlative of ἄτιμος ‘without honour’, so ‘most dishonoured’; she asks to learn how little her son and she count with Zeus. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Her, greatly vexed, addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed, be troubled’, with μέγα ‘greatly’; the same verb returns for the gods at 570. Zeus is annoyed, not grieved: he is being drawn into a quarrel with Hera. The rest is the stock introduction: τὴν ‘her’, προσέφη ‘addressed’, νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’.

sentences.t:
ἦ δὴ λοίγια ἔργ’ ὅ τέ μ’ ἐχθοδοπῆσαι ἐφήσεις
Ἥρῃ ὅτ’ ἄν μ’ ἐρέθῃσιν ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσιν·
sentences.tr:
ē dē loigia erg’ ho te m’ echthodopēsai ephēseis
Hērēi hot’ an m’ erethēisin oneideiois epeessin·
sentences.l:
“Truly, ruin-bringing deeds these are, that you will set me to be at enmity
with Hera, whenever she provokes me with words of reproach;
sentences.i: “This is a disastrous business, that you will set me at odds with Hera, whenever she provokes me with words of reproach;
sentences.n: Zeus is exasperated. ἦ δή ‘truly’ opens an exclamation with no verb: λοίγια ἔργα ‘ruin-bringing deeds’ (λοιγός ‘ruin’, as at 341), that is, a business that can end only badly. ὅ τέ is read ‘in that, because’. ἐχθοδοπῆσαι is a rare verb, ‘be at enmity, quarrel’, an infinitive after ἐφήσεις, the future of ἐφίημι ‘send upon, set to’, so ‘you will set me at enmity’. ὅτ’ ἄν with the subjunctive ἐρέθῃσιν (ἐρέθω, a by-form of ἐρεθίζω ‘provoke’, as at 32) is ‘whenever she provokes’. ὀνειδείοις ἐπέεσσιν ‘words of reproach’ is a formula.

sentences.t:
ἣ δὲ καὶ αὔτως μ’ αἰεὶ ἐν ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι
νεικεῖ, καί τέ μέ φησι μάχῃ Τρώεσσιν ἀρήγειν.
sentences.tr:
hē de kai autōs m’ aiei en athanatoisi theoisi
neikei, kai te me phēsi machēi Trōessin arēgein.
sentences.l:
and she, even just so, always among the immortal gods
rebukes me, and says that I in battle help the Trojans.
sentences.i: She is always rebuking me among the immortal gods, even without cause, and says that I help the Trojans in battle.
sentences.n: αὔτως ‘just so, for nothing’: she scolds him without waiting for a cause. νεικεῖ is the contracted νεικέει from νεικέω ‘rebuke’. καί τέ … φησι is ‘and says’ (τέ is the epic enclitic), with the infinitive ἀρήγειν ‘to help’ and the accusative μέ as its subject; ἀρήγειν takes the dative Τρώεσσιν ‘the Trojans’, as at 408. μάχῃ is ‘in battle’, a dative.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν αὖτις ἀπόστιχε μή τι νοήσῃ
Ἥρη· ἐμοὶ δέ κε ταῦτα μελήσεται ὄφρα τελέσσω·
sentences.tr:
alla sy men nyn autis apostiche mē ti noēsēi
Hērē· emoi de ke tauta melēsetai ophra telessō·
sentences.l:
But you for now go away again, lest she notice anything,
Hera; and to me these things will be a care, until I accomplish them;
sentences.i: But for now go away again, so that Hera notices nothing; these matters will be my concern, until I have accomplished them;
sentences.n: Zeus sends her off. μή τι νοήσῃ is a negative purpose clause, ‘lest she notice anything’ (νοέω ‘perceive’), with its subject Ἥρη held back to the start of the next line; ἀπόστιχε is the imperative of ἀποστείχω ‘go away’. ἐμοὶ δέ κε ταῦτα μελήσεται is ‘to me these things will be a care’ (μέλω, with κε), and ὄφρα τελέσσω, ὄφρα with the aorist subjunctive, is ‘until I accomplish them’ (it could also be read ‘so that I may accomplish’).

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ ἄγε τοι κεφαλῇ κατανεύσομαι ὄφρα πεποίθῃς·
sentences.tr: ei d’ age toi kephalēi kataneusomai ophra pepoithēis·
sentences.l: But come, to you with my head I will nod assent, so that you may be sure;
sentences.i: But come, I will nod my head to you in assent, so that you may be sure;
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἄγε is ‘but come’ (as at 302); the εἰ is part of the idiom. κατανεύσομαι is the future middle of κατανεύω, ‘I will nod assent’, with κεφαλῇ ‘with my head’. πεποίθῃς is the perfect subjunctive of πείθω in its intransitive sense, ‘be persuaded, trust’: ‘so that you may be sure’.

sentences.t:
τοῦτο γὰρ ἐξ ἐμέθεν γε μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι μέγιστον
τέκμωρ·
sentences.tr:
touto gar ex emethen ge met’ athanatoisi megiston
tekmōr·
sentences.l:
For this from me, among the immortals, is the greatest
sign;
sentences.i: for among the immortals this is the greatest sign that comes from me:
sentences.n: τέκμωρ is a fixed sign or pledge, here the nod as proof of a promise (the Odyssey uses the same word for ‘a way out’, an end). ἐξ ἐμέθεν is ‘from me’, with the epic ending -θεν for the genitive, and μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι ‘among the immortals’. There is no verb; ‘this is’ is understood. The next unit says what makes the sign good.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐμὸν παλινάγρετον οὐδ’ ἀπατηλὸν
οὐδ’ ἀτελεύτητον ὅ τί κεν κεφαλῇ κατανεύσω.
sentences.tr:
ou gar emon palinagreton oud’ apatēlon
oud’ ateleutēton ho ti ken kephalēi kataneusō.
sentences.l:
for nothing of mine can be taken back, nor is deceptive,
nor unfulfilled, whatever I nod assent to with my head.”
sentences.i: for whatever I nod my assent to with my head can never be taken back, or prove false, or go unfulfilled.”
sentences.n: A solemn guarantee. ἐμόν is the neuter ‘what is mine’, and the three adjectives all describe the one thing nodded to: παλινάγρετον ‘that can be taken back’ (παλίν ‘back’ with a verbal adjective of αἱρέω ‘take’), ἀπατηλόν ‘deceptive’ (ἀπάτη ‘deceit’), ἀτελεύτητον ‘unfulfilled’ (ἀ- + τελευτάω ‘bring to an end’). ὅ τί κεν … κατανεύσω is a general clause, ‘whatever I nod assent to’. Zeus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ κυανέῃσιν ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι νεῦσε Κρονίων·
sentences.tr: ē kai kyaneēisin ep’ ophrysi neuse Kroniōn·
sentences.l: He spoke, and on his dark brows nodded the son of Cronus;
sentences.i: So he said, and the son of Cronus nodded with his dark brows;
sentences.n: ἦ καί ‘he spoke, and’ closes the speech and starts the act. κυανέῃσιν is the feminine dative plural of κυάνεος ‘dark’ (dark blue), with ὀφρύσι ‘brows’, and ἐπ’ ὀφρύσι is ‘with, on his brows’. νεῦσε is the aorist of νεύω ‘nod’; this is the nod he promised at 524. Κρονίων is the patronymic, ‘son of Cronus’, here Zeus.

sentences.t:
ἀμβρόσιαι δ’ ἄρα χαῖται ἐπερρώσαντο ἄνακτος
κρατὸς ἀπ’ ἀθανάτοιο·
sentences.tr:
ambrosiai d’ ara chaitai eperrōsanto anaktos
kratos ap’ athanatoio·
sentences.l:
and ambrosial locks streamed forward, of the lord,
from his immortal head;
sentences.i: and the ambrosial locks of the lord streamed forward from his immortal head;
sentences.n: ἀμβρόσιαι ‘ambrosial’ (of the gods’ own substance, from ἄμβροτος ‘deathless’) goes with χαῖται ‘locks, hair’. ἐπερρώσαντο is the aorist of ἐπιρρώομαι ‘rush on, stream forward’: the hair moves as the head nods. ἄνακτος ‘of the lord’ is a genitive with χαῖται, ‘the lord’s locks’, and κρατός is the old genitive of κάρη ‘head’. ἀπ’ is ἀπό ‘from’, with the elision.

sentences.t: μέγαν δ’ ἐλέλιξεν Ὄλυμπον.
sentences.tr: megan d’ elelixen Olympon.
sentences.l: and he shook great Olympus.
sentences.i: and he shook great Olympus.
sentences.n: ἐλέλιξεν is the aorist of ἐλελίζω ‘make shake, make quiver’, here transitive: the nod shakes the mountain, which is also the home of the gods. The shaking is the poet’s sign that the promise is binding.

sentences.t: τώ γ’ ὣς βουλεύσαντε διέτμαγεν·
sentences.tr: tō g’ hōs bouleusante dietmagen·
sentences.l: The two, having so taken counsel, parted;
sentences.i: Having made their plan in this way, the two parted;
sentences.n: τώ is the dual ‘the two’ (Thetis and Zeus), and γ’ stresses it. βουλεύσαντε is the dual aorist participle of βουλεύω ‘take counsel, plan’, and διέτμαγεν ‘they parted’ is the aorist passive of διατμήγω ‘cut apart’ (‘were cut apart’).

sentences.t:
ἣ μὲν ἔπειτα
εἰς ἅλα ἆλτο βαθεῖαν ἀπ’ αἰγλήεντος Ὀλύμπου,
Ζεὺς δὲ ἑὸν πρὸς δῶμα·
sentences.tr:
hē men epeita
eis hala alto batheian ap’ aiglēentos Olympou,
Zeus de heon pros dōma·
sentences.i: She then leapt from light-filled Olympus into the deep sea, and Zeus went to his own house;
sentences.n: ἣ μὲν … Ζεὺς δὲ sets the two departures side by side, and the verb of the second half is understood (‘went’). ἅλα is the accusative of ἅλς ‘sea’, and ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’: Thetis dives back into her father’s sea. αἰγλήεντος is the genitive of αἰγλήεις ‘light-filled’ (αἴγλη ‘gleam’), the Odyssey’s word for Olympus (20.103). ἑόν is the epic possessive ‘his own’.

sentences.t:
θεοὶ δ’ ἅμα πάντες ἀνέσταν
ἐξ ἑδέων σφοῦ πατρὸς ἐναντίον·
sentences.tr:
theoi d’ hama pantes anestan
ex hedeōn sphou patros enantion·
sentences.l:
and the gods all together stood up
from their seats before their own father;
sentences.i: and all the gods rose together from their seats in front of their father;
sentences.n: ἀνέσταν is the aorist of ἀνίστημι in its intransitive sense, ‘stood up’, with the ending -αν for -ησαν. ἑδέων is the genitive plural of ἕδος ‘seat’, and σφοῦ the possessive σφός ‘their own’. ἐναντίον with the genitive is ‘in front of, in the presence of’: the gods stand as Zeus enters, which is the courtesy due to a father.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τις ἔτλη
μεῖναι ἐπερχόμενον, ἀλλ’ ἀντίοι ἔσταν ἅπαντες.
sentences.tr:
oude tis etlē
meinai eperchomenon, all’ antioi estan hapantes.
sentences.l:
and none dared
to await him as he came on, but facing him they stood, all of them.
sentences.i: and not one of them dared to wait for him as he came on, but all of them stood to face him.
sentences.n: οὐδέ τις ἔτλη + infinitive is ‘and none dared’ (τλάω, as in τέτληκας at 228); no one stayed seated while he came on. ἐπερχόμενον is the participle of ἐπέρχομαι ‘come on’, agreeing with ‘him’ understood. ἀντίοι ‘facing’ is nominative plural, and ἔσταν ‘they stood’ is the aorist of ἵστημι in its intransitive form.

sentences.t: ὣς ὃ μὲν ἔνθα καθέζετ’ ἐπὶ θρόνου·
sentences.tr: hōs ho men entha kathezet’ epi thronou·
sentences.l: So he there sat down upon his throne;
sentences.i: So he sat down there on his throne;
sentences.n: ὣς … ἔνθα is ‘so, in that way (with the gods standing), there’. ὃ μέν ‘he for his part’ sets Zeus against Hera, who comes next. καθέζετ’ is the imperfect of καθέζομαι ‘sit down’, and ἐπὶ θρόνου ‘upon his throne’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μιν Ἥρη
ἠγνοίησεν ἰδοῦσ’ ὅτι οἱ συμφράσσατο βουλὰς
ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος.
sentences.tr:
oude min Hērē
ēgnoiēsen idous’ hoti hoi symphrassato boulas
argyropeza Thetis thygatēr halioio gerontos.
sentences.l:
and Hera, on seeing him, did not
fail to recognize that with him had devised plans
silver-footed Thetis, daughter of the old man of the sea.
sentences.i: And Hera, when she saw him, did not fail to know that silver-footed Thetis, the daughter of the old man of the sea, had been devising plans with him.
sentences.n: Hera saw what the other gods did not. μιν ‘him’ is the object of ἰδοῦσ’ ‘seeing’ (aorist participle of ὁράω), and ἠγνοίησεν is the aorist of ἀγνοιέω ‘fail to know’; with οὐδέ the sense is ‘did not fail to know’, the Odyssey’s English for the same formula (5.77), here followed by a clause with ὅτι ‘that’. οἱ is the epic dative ‘with him’, with συμφράσσατο ‘devised together’ (aorist middle of συμφράζομαι); βουλάς ‘plans’. ἀργυρόπεζα ‘silver-footed’ is Thetis’ stock epithet (the Odyssey has it, 24.92), and ἁλίοιο γέροντος ‘the old man of the sea’, her father, is not named here.

sentences.t: αὐτίκα κερτομίοισι Δία Κρονίωνα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: autika kertomioisi Dia Kroniōna prosēuda·
sentences.l: At once with taunting ones she spoke to Zeus, the son of Cronus:
sentences.i: At once she spoke to Zeus, the son of Cronus, with taunts:
sentences.n: κερτομίοισι is an adjective used alone for ‘with taunting words’, the noun ἐπέεσσι being understood, as in the Odyssey (9.474). Δία is the accusative of Ζεύς, with Κρονίωνα ‘son of Cronus’. Hera is the unstated subject, named just before. προσηύδα ‘spoke to’ is the imperfect of προσαυδάω.

sentences.t: τίς δ’ αὖ τοι δολομῆτα θεῶν συμφράσσατο βουλάς;
sentences.tr: tis d’ au toi dolomēta theōn symphrassato boulas;
sentences.l: “Which again of the gods, you of guileful counsel, has devised plans with you?
sentences.i: “Which of the gods, you of guileful counsel, has been devising plans with you this time?
sentences.n: Hera mocks him. τίς … θεῶν is ‘which of the gods?’, with αὖ ‘again, this time’ and τοι ‘with you’ (the enclitic dative of σύ). δολομῆτα is the vocative of δολομήτης ‘of guileful counsel’ (δόλος ‘guile’ + μῆτις ‘counsel’), a by-form of the δολόμητις that the Odyssey gives Aegisthus; here it is her taunt. συμφράσσατο βουλάς ‘devised plans together’ repeats the verb of 537.

sentences.t:
αἰεί τοι φίλον ἐστὶν ἐμεῦ ἀπὸ νόσφιν ἐόντα
κρυπτάδια φρονέοντα δικαζέμεν·
sentences.tr:
aiei toi philon estin emeu apo nosphin eonta
kryptadia phroneonta dikazemen·
sentences.l:
Always to you it is dear, being away from me,
thinking secret things, to give judgement;
sentences.i: It is always dear to you, keeping apart from me, to think your secret thoughts and pass judgement on them;
sentences.n: φίλον ἐστίν ‘it is dear, it pleases’ takes the dative τοι ‘to you’, and the infinitive δικαζέμεν (epic -έμεν for -ειν) ‘to give judgement, decide’ is what pleases him. ἐόντα and φρονέοντα are accusatives agreeing with the subject of the infinitive left unexpressed: ‘you, being apart … thinking’. ἐμεῦ ἀπὸ νόσφιν is ‘apart from me’ (ἐμεῦ the epic genitive, νόσφιν an adverb). κρυπτάδια is the neuter plural ‘secret things’, and φρονέω ‘think’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τί πώ μοι
πρόφρων τέτληκας εἰπεῖν ἔπος ὅττι νοήσῃς.
sentences.tr:
oude ti pō moi
prophrōn tetlēkas eipein epos hotti noēsēis.
sentences.l:
and never yet to me
ready-minded have you dared to say a word of what you have in mind.”
sentences.i: and you have never yet dared, with a ready mind, to tell me a word of what you are thinking.”
sentences.n: οὐδέ τί πώ is ‘and not yet at all’. τέτληκας is the perfect of τλάω ‘dare’ with the infinitive εἰπεῖν ‘to say’: ‘you have never dared’ (as at 228). πρόφρων ‘with a ready mind’ (πρό + φρήν) is the Odyssey’s word, ‘willing, whole-hearted’, and here bitter: he never tells her willingly. ὅττι is the epic form of ὅ τι ‘whatever’, with the subjunctive νοήσῃς ‘you may have in mind’. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita patēr andrōn te theōn te·
sentences.l: Her then answered the father of men and of gods:
sentences.i: Then the father of men and of gods answered her:
sentences.n: A reply-formula whose speaker, Zeus, is named by his title πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε ‘father of men and of gods’. ἠμείβετ’ is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and τὴν is the article used as ‘her’.

sentences.t:
Ἥρη μὴ δὴ πάντας ἐμοὺς ἐπιέλπεο μύθους
εἰδήσειν· χαλεποί τοι ἔσοντ’ ἀλόχῳ περ ἐούσῃ·
sentences.tr:
Hērē mē dē pantas emous epielpeo mythous
eidēsein· chalepoi toi esont’ alochōi per eousēi·
sentences.l:
“Hera, do not now hope all my words
to know; hard for you will they be, even though a wife you are;
sentences.i: “Hera, do not hope to know all my words; they will be hard for you, even though you are my wife;
sentences.n: μὴ … ἐπιέλπεο is a prohibition with the present imperative of ἐπιέλπομαι ‘hope for, expect’; its infinitive εἰδήσειν (future of οἶδα, ‘to know’) takes πάντας … μύθους ‘all my words’ as object. χαλεποί ‘hard’ (to bear or to know). ἔσοντ’ is ἔσονται, the epic future of εἰμί. ἀλόχῳ περ ἐούσῃ is ‘even though you are a wife’ (περ ‘even though’, the dative agreeing with τοι); ἄλοχος is ‘wife’ as in the Odyssey.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὃν μέν κ’ ἐπιεικὲς ἀκουέμεν οὔ τις ἔπειτα
οὔτε θεῶν πρότερος τὸν εἴσεται οὔτ’ ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.tr:
all’ hon men k’ epieikes akouemen ou tis epeita
oute theōn proteros ton eisetai out’ anthrōpōn·
sentences.l:
but whichever it is fitting to hear, no one then
will know it earlier, neither of gods nor of men;
sentences.i: but any word that it is fitting for you to hear, no one will know before you, neither of the gods nor of men;
sentences.n: ὃν μέν … τόν is ‘whichever … that one’, the noun to be supplied being μῦθον ‘word’ from 545 (it is masculine). ὃν μέν κ’ ἐπιεικὲς ἀκουέμεν is ‘whichever it is fitting to hear’, with κε, the adjective ἐπιεικές ‘fitting, suitable’ and the infinitive ἀκουέμεν (epic for ἀκούειν). πρότερος ‘earlier’ is the comparative adjective, English ‘before you’. οὔ τις … οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘no one, neither … nor’, and εἴσεται is the future of οἶδα.

sentences.t:
ὃν δέ κ’ ἐγὼν ἀπάνευθε θεῶν ἐθέλωμι νοῆσαι
μή τι σὺ ταῦτα ἕκαστα διείρεο μηδὲ μετάλλα.
sentences.tr:
hon de k’ egōn apaneuthe theōn ethelōmi noēsai
mē ti sy tauta hekasta dieireo mēde metalla.
sentences.l:
but whichever I, apart from the gods, may wish to think out,
not at all do you question about each of these things, nor inquire.”
sentences.i: but whatever I choose to think out apart from the gods, do not question me about each detail of it, or inquire.”
sentences.n: ὃν δέ κ’ … ‘but whichever’ (word, again μῦθον) answers the ὃν μέν of 547. ἐγών is the epic ἐγώ, ἀπάνευθε θεῶν ‘apart from the gods’, ἐθέλωμι the subjunctive with κε ‘I may wish’, and νοῆσαι ‘to think out, plan’. μή τι … διείρεο μηδὲ μετάλλα is a prohibition with imperatives: διείρεο is the imperative of διείρομαι ‘question closely’ (compare εἴρομαι ‘ask’ at 553), and μετάλλα that of μεταλλάω ‘inquire’. ταῦτα ἕκαστα is ‘each of these things’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita boōpis potnia Hērē·
sentences.l: Him then answered ox-eyed lady Hera:
sentences.i: Then ox-eyed lady Hera answered him:
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is masculine, as τὴν was feminine at 544: Zeus is now the one answered. βοῶπις ‘ox-eyed’ (βοῦς ‘ox’ + ὤψ ‘eye’) is Hera’s stock epithet; the usual explanation is large, calm eyes like an ox’s, but the Greek does not say. πότνια is ‘lady’, as in the Odyssey.

sentences.t: αἰνότατε Κρονίδη ποῖον τὸν μῦθον ἔειπες;
sentences.tr: ainotate Kronidē poion ton mython eeipes;
sentences.l: “Most dread son of Cronus, what sort of word is this you have spoken?
sentences.i: “Most dreadful son of Cronus, what kind of word is this that you have spoken?
sentences.n: αἰνότατε is the vocative of αἰνότατος, the superlative of αἰνός ‘dread’ (αἰνά at 414), sharp rather than respectful. Κρονίδη is the patronymic vocative, ‘son of Cronus’. ποῖον τὸν μῦθον is ‘what sort of word (is) this word’, the article giving the sense ‘this’; ἔειπες is the aorist of εἶπον ‘say’ in its epic form with doubled ε.

sentences.t:
καὶ λίην σε πάρος γ’ οὔτ’ εἴρομαι οὔτε μεταλλῶ,
ἀλλὰ μάλ’ εὔκηλος τὰ φράζεαι ἅσσ’ ἐθέλῃσθα.
sentences.tr:
kai liēn se paros g’ out’ eiromai oute metallō,
alla mal’ eukēlos ta phrazeai hass’ ethelēistha.
sentences.l:
Truly, before now at least, I neither ask you nor inquire,
but quite at ease you plan the things that you wish.
sentences.i: Truly, until now I have neither asked you questions nor pried, but you plan whatever you please quite at your ease.
sentences.n: Hera says she has not been a prying wife. καὶ λίην is ‘and truly, quite so’, an intensifier (λίην ‘very’), and πάρος γε ‘before now at least’. οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, with the present εἴρομαι ‘I ask’ and μεταλλῶ (contracted from μεταλλάω) ‘I inquire’, as in 550. εὔκηλος ‘at ease, undisturbed’ is the adjective used as an adverb. φράζεαι is the epic second singular of φράζομαι ‘consider, plan’; ἅσσα is ἅτινα ‘whatever things’, with the subjunctive ἐθέλῃσθα, in the old second-singular ending -σθα, ‘you may wish’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ αἰνῶς δείδοικα κατὰ φρένα μή σε παρείπῃ
ἀργυρόπεζα Θέτις θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος·
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ ainōs deidoika kata phrena mē se pareipēi
argyropeza Thetis thygatēr halioio gerontos·
sentences.l:
But now I fear dreadfully in my mind lest she win you over,
silver-footed Thetis, daughter of the old man of the sea;
sentences.i: But now I am dreadfully afraid in my mind that she has talked you round, silver-footed Thetis, the daughter of the old man of the sea;
sentences.n: αἰνῶς ‘dreadfully’ is the adverb of αἰνός; δείδοικα is the perfect of δείδω ‘fear’, with κατὰ φρένα ‘in my mind’. μή σε παρείπῃ is the fear clause, ‘lest she win you over’: παρείπῃ is the aorist subjunctive of παρεῖπον ‘win over with words’ (the same stem as παράφημι at 577). The subject, held back to the next line, is Thetis, with the epithet and father of 538.

sentences.t: ἠερίη γὰρ σοί γε παρέζετο καὶ λάβε γούνων·
sentences.tr: ēeriē gar soi ge parezeto kai labe gounōn·
sentences.l: for morning-early she sat beside you and took hold of your knees;
sentences.i: for early in the morning she sat down beside you and took hold of your knees;
sentences.n: She gives her reason. ἠερίη is read ‘early in the morning’ (compare 497, where Thetis went up to Olympus ἠερίη), though another reading takes it from ἀήρ ‘mist’, ‘in the mist’; the sense is not certain. σοί γε is ‘beside you’, with the emphatic γε. παρέζετο is the imperfect of παρέζομαι ‘sit beside’, and λάβε γούνων ‘took hold of the knees’ is the suppliant’s grip, as at 500, with the genitive of the part held.

sentences.t:
τῇ σ’ ὀΐω κατανεῦσαι ἐτήτυμον ὡς Ἀχιλῆα
τιμήσῃς, ὀλέσῃς δὲ πολέας ἐπὶ νηυσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
tēi s’ oïō kataneusai etētymon hōs Achilēa
timēsēis, olesēis de poleas epi nēusin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
To her, I suspect, you nodded assent, in truth, that Achilles
you will honour, and destroy many beside the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: I suspect that you nodded your assent to her in truth, that you will honour Achilles and destroy many beside the ships of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: τῇ is the article used as a pronoun, ‘to her’, and σ’ is σε. ὀΐω ‘I suspect’ is nearly parenthetical, with the infinitive κατανεῦσαι ‘to have nodded assent’. ἐτήτυμον ‘in truth’ is a neuter adjective used as an adverb. ὡς … τιμήσῃς, ὀλέσῃς is what the nod was for, ὡς with the subjunctive, ‘that you will honour … and destroy’; πολέας is the epic accusative plural of πολύς ‘many’. Her speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenos prosephē nephelēgereta Zeus·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: The stock reply-formula, the same line as in the Odyssey (1.63): ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’, προσέφη ‘addressed’, νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς ‘cloud-gatherer Zeus’, with τὴν ‘her’ naming Hera as the one answered.

sentences.t: δαιμονίη αἰεὶ μὲν ὀΐεαι οὐδέ σε λήθω·
sentences.tr: daimoniē aiei men oïeai oude se lēthō·
sentences.l: “Strange woman, always you suspect, and I escape not your notice;
sentences.i: “Strange woman, you are always suspecting, and I never escape your notice;
sentences.n: δαιμονίη is the feminine vocative of δαιμόνιος, a puzzling address, ‘strange one’ or ‘possessed one’, said to someone whose behaviour the speaker cannot make out. ὀΐεαι is the epic second singular of ὀΐομαι ‘suspect’ (ὀΐω at 558), and οὐδέ σε λήθω is ‘nor do I escape your notice’ (λανθάνω with the accusative σε).

sentences.t:
πρῆξαι δ’ ἔμπης οὔ τι δυνήσεαι, ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ θυμοῦ
μᾶλλον ἐμοὶ ἔσεαι·
sentences.tr:
prēxai d’ empēs ou ti dynēseai, all’ apo thymou
mallon emoi eseai·
sentences.l:
but to accomplish anything you will not be able all the same, but from my heart
the more you will be to me;
sentences.i: all the same you will not be able to accomplish anything, but will only be the farther from my heart;
sentences.n: πρῆξαι is the aorist infinitive of πράσσω ‘accomplish’ after δυνήσεαι, the epic future of δύναμαι ‘you will be able’; ἔμπης ‘all the same’. ἀπὸ θυμοῦ ἐμοὶ ἔσεαι is ‘you will be away from my heart, for me’, that is, out of his affection, and μᾶλλον ‘the more’. ἔσεαι is the epic future of εἰμί.

sentences.t: τὸ δέ τοι καὶ ῥίγιον ἔσται.
sentences.tr: to de toi kai rhigion estai.
sentences.l: and that for you will be even worse.
sentences.i: and that will be worse still for you.
sentences.n: ῥίγιον is the comparative of a word for cold or chill (ῥῖγος ‘cold’), used as ‘worse, harder to bear’; the same phrase stands at 325 of the man in Agamemnon’s threat, and the Odyssey uses it both of evening cold and of what is worse. τοι is ‘for you’.

sentences.t: εἰ δ’ οὕτω τοῦτ’ ἐστὶν ἐμοὶ μέλλει φίλον εἶναι·
sentences.tr: ei d’ houtō tout’ estin emoi mellei philon einai·
sentences.l: But if this is so, it is sure to be dear to me;
sentences.i: But if that is how it is, then it must be what pleases me;
sentences.n: Zeus waves her suspicion aside. εἰ … οὕτω τοῦτ’ ἐστίν is ‘if this is so (as you think)’, and ἐμοὶ μέλλει φίλον εἶναι is ‘it is bound to be dear to me’, with μέλλω and the infinitive for what is bound to be: ‘so be it, it must be my wish’. The line is tight, and the sense is a shrug.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἀκέουσα κάθησο, ἐμῷ δ’ ἐπιπείθεο μύθῳ,
sentences.tr: all’ akeousa kathēso, emōi d’ epipeitheo mythōi,
sentences.l: But sit in silence, and obey my word,
sentences.i: So sit in silence, and obey my word,
sentences.n: ἀκέουσα is the feminine of ἀκέων ‘in silence’ (511), and κάθησο the imperative of κάθημαι ‘sit’; ‘sit’ is the whole command, she is to stay where she is. ἐπιπείθεο is the imperative middle of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey’, with the dative μύθῳ ‘word’ and ἐμῷ ‘my’.

sentences.t:
μή νύ τοι οὐ χραίσμωσιν ὅσοι θεοί εἰσ’ ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ
ἆσσον ἰόνθ’, ὅτε κέν τοι ἀάπτους χεῖρας ἐφείω.
sentences.tr:
mē ny toi ou chraismōsin hosoi theoi eis’ en Olympōi
asson ionth’, hote ken toi aaptous cheiras epheiō.
sentences.l:
lest all as many gods as are on Olympus fail to avail you
as I come near, when I lay my untouchable hands on you.”
sentences.i: lest all the gods on Olympus fail to help you when I come near and lay my irresistible hands on you.”
sentences.n: μή νυ … οὐ with the subjunctive is a warning, ‘lest … fail to’: μή states the fear and οὐ negates the verb, so there is no double negative. χραίσμωσιν is the aorist subjunctive of χραισμέω ‘avail, help’ (as at 589), with the dative τοι ‘you’. ὅσοι θεοί εἰσ’ ἐν Ὀλύμπῳ is ‘as many gods as are on Olympus’ (εἰσ’ is εἰσί). ἰόνθ’ is the elided accusative singular of the participle of εἶμι ‘go’, agreeing with ‘me’ understood, and ἆσσον ‘nearer’. ἐφείω is the aorist subjunctive of ἐφίημι ‘lay upon’ (compare ἐφήσεις at 518), with χεῖρας ‘hands’. ἀάπτους is an old word whose meaning is not known; ‘irresistible’ (in the translation) and ‘untouchable’ (in the literal line) are two ancient guesses. Zeus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ ἔδεισεν δὲ βοῶπις πότνια Ἥρη,
καί ῥ’ ἀκέουσα καθῆστο ἐπιγνάμψασα φίλον κῆρ·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’ edeisen de boōpis potnia Hērē,
kai rh’ akeousa kathēsto epignampsasa philon kēr·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and was afraid, ox-eyed lady Hera,
and she sat in silence, having bent her dear heart;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and ox-eyed lady Hera was afraid, and sat in silence, having forced her dear heart to yield;
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατο, the imperfect middle of φημί, its last vowel elided). ἔδεισεν is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’ (as in δείδοικα at 555). καθῆστο is the imperfect of κάθημαι ‘sat’, now obeying the κάθησο of 565. ἐπιγνάμψασα is the aorist participle of ἐπιγνάμπτω ‘bend’: she bends her own heart, that is, makes it yield against its wish. κῆρ is ‘heart’.

sentences.t: ὄχθησαν δ’ ἀνὰ δῶμα Διὸς θεοὶ Οὐρανίωνες·
sentences.tr: ochthēsan d’ ana dōma Dios theoi Ouraniōnes·
sentences.l: and were vexed, throughout the house of Zeus, the gods, the children of Heaven;
sentences.i: and throughout the house of Zeus the gods, the children of Heaven, were troubled;
sentences.n: ὄχθησαν is the aorist of ὀχθέω ‘be vexed’ (compare ὀχθήσας at 517): the whole of Olympus is uneasy at the quarrel. ἀνὰ δῶμα with the accusative is ‘throughout the house’. Οὐρανίωνες ‘children of Heaven’ (Οὐρανός) is the Odyssey’s epithet for the gods, and may mean ‘descendants of Uranus’ or ‘dwellers in heaven’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσιν δ’ Ἥφαιστος κλυτοτέχνης ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν
μητρὶ φίλῃ ἐπίηρα φέρων λευκωλένῳ Ἥρῃ·
sentences.tr:
toisin d’ Hēphaistos klytotechnēs ērch’ agoreuein
mētri philēi epiēra pherōn leukōlenōi Hērēi·
sentences.l:
and among them Hephaestus, famous in craft, began to speak,
bringing pleasing things to his dear mother, white-armed Hera:
sentences.i: and Hephaestus, famous in craft, was the first to speak among them, trying to please his dear mother, white-armed Hera:
sentences.n: Hephaestus is the craftsman god, son of Zeus and Hera, and he takes up the peacemaker’s part. τοῖσιν ‘among them’ (the gods); κλυτοτέχνης ‘famous in craft’ (κλυτός ‘famous’ + τέχνη ‘craft’) is his stock epithet. ἦρχ’ ἀγορεύειν is ‘began to speak’, ἦρχε with the infinitive. ἐπίηρα φέρων is an idiom, ‘bringing pleasing things’, that is, doing what pleases (ἐπίηρος ‘pleasing’), and returns at 578. μητρὶ … Ἥρῃ are datives, ‘to his mother Hera’; λευκωλένῳ is ‘white-armed’.

sentences.t:
ἦ δὴ λοίγια ἔργα τάδ’ ἔσσεται οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἀνεκτά,
εἰ δὴ σφὼ ἕνεκα θνητῶν ἐριδαίνετον ὧδε,
sentences.tr:
ē dē loigia erga tad’ essetai oud’ et’ anekta,
ei dē sphō heneka thnētōn eridaineton hōde,
sentences.l:
“Truly ruin-bringing deeds these will be, and no longer bearable,
if indeed you two for the sake of mortals quarrel thus,
sentences.i: “This will be a disastrous business, and no longer to be borne, if you two quarrel like this for the sake of mortals,
sentences.n: ἦ δὴ λοίγια ἔργα repeats Zeus’ own words of 518, now in Hephaestus’ mouth: the same grim business. τάδ’ ἔσσεται is ‘these will be’ (ἔσσεται the epic future of εἰμί), and οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἀνεκτά ‘no longer bearable’ (ἀνέχομαι ‘bear’). εἰ δή … ἐριδαίνετον is ‘if indeed you two quarrel’: σφώ is the dual ‘you two’ and ἐριδαίνετον the dual of ἐριδαίνω ‘quarrel’. ἕνεκα θνητῶν is ‘for the sake of mortals’, and ὧδε ‘thus’.

sentences.t: ἐν δὲ θεοῖσι κολῳὸν ἐλαύνετον·
sentences.tr: en de theoisi kolōion elauneton·
sentences.l: and among the gods an uproar you two drive on;
sentences.i: and keep an uproar going among the gods;
sentences.n: κολῳός is a noisy wrangle, an uproar; the word is rare, and the context fixes the sense. ἐλαύνετον is the dual of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, here ‘keep going, stir up’, and ἐν … θεοῖσι is ‘among the gods’.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τι δαιτὸς
ἐσθλῆς ἔσσεται ἦδος, ἐπεὶ τὰ χερείονα νικᾷ.
sentences.tr:
oude ti daitos
esthlēs essetai ēdos, epei ta chereiona nikāi.
sentences.l:
and not at all of a feast
good will there be pleasure, since the worse things win.
sentences.i: and there will be no pleasure at all in a good feast, since the worse side is winning.
sentences.n: These words are the Odyssey’s, said there of the quarrel over the beggar (18.403). ἦδος is ‘pleasure’, δαιτὸς ἐσθλῆς ‘a good feast’, and τὰ χερείονα ‘the worse (things)’ is neuter, ‘the worse side’; ἔσσεται is the future ‘will be’.

sentences.t:
μητρὶ δ’ ἐγὼ παράφημι καὶ αὐτῇ περ νοεούσῃ
πατρὶ φίλῳ ἐπίηρα φέρειν Διί,
sentences.tr:
mētri d’ egō paraphēmi kai autēi per noeousēi
patri philōi epiēra pherein Dii,
sentences.l:
and to my mother I give counsel, though she herself understands,
to bring pleasing things to my dear father, Zeus,
sentences.i: And I advise my mother, though she herself understands, to please my dear father Zeus,
sentences.n: παράφημι is the first-person present of παράφημι ‘advise, speak to persuade’ (compare παρείπῃ at 555), with the dative μητρί ‘to my mother’; δ’ ἐγώ ‘and I’ sets his advice against the quarrel. αὐτῇ περ νοεούσῃ is ‘even though she herself understands’ (the dative participle agrees with μητρί): she already knows what he will say. ἐπίηρα φέρειν Διί is ‘to bring pleasing things to Zeus’ (compare 572), and πατρὶ φίλῳ ‘to my dear father’.

sentences.t:
ὄφρα μὴ αὖτε
νεικείῃσι πατήρ, σὺν δ’ ἡμῖν δαῖτα ταράξῃ.
sentences.tr:
ophra mē aute
neikeiēisi patēr, syn d’ hēmin daita taraxēi.
sentences.l:
so that not again
the father may rebuke, and for us confound the feast.
sentences.i: so that our father may not rebuke again and throw the feast into confusion for us.
sentences.n: ὄφρα μή + subjunctive is a negative purpose clause, ‘so that … not’; νεικείῃσι is the subjunctive νεικείῃ with the old ending -σι, from νεικέω ‘rebuke’ (as νεικεῖ at 521). The Greek gives no object; it is plainly Hera. σύν … ταράξῃ is the verb ταράσσω ‘stir up, confound’ with σύν split off from it, ‘throw into confusion’; ἡμῖν is ‘for us’.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ κ’ ἐθέλῃσιν Ὀλύμπιος ἀστεροπητὴς
ἐξ ἑδέων στυφελίξαι·
sentences.tr:
ei per gar k’ ethelēisin Olympios asteropētēs
ex hedeōn styphelixai·
sentences.l:
For if he should wish, the Olympian, the lightning-flasher,
to thrust us from our seats—
sentences.i: For if the Olympian who flashes lightning should wish to drive us from our seats—
sentences.n: A sentence left unfinished: ‘if he wishes … (he can)’. The speaker stops because the thought, that Zeus could throw them all out, needs no completing. Ὀλύμπιος ‘the Olympian’ alone means Zeus (again at 583 and 589), and ἀστεροπητής ‘lightning-flasher’ is his stock epithet (ἀστεροπή ‘lightning’), repeated at 609. ἐθέλῃσιν is the subjunctive with εἴ … κε, ‘should wish’, and στυφελίξαι the aorist infinitive of στυφελίζω ‘strike hard, thrust out’; ἐξ ἑδέων ‘from our seats’ (compare 534).

sentences.t: ὃ γὰρ πολὺ φέρτατός ἐστιν.
sentences.tr: ho gar poly phertatos estin.
sentences.l: for he is by far the best.
sentences.i: for he is by far the best of us.
sentences.n: φέρτατος is the superlative of φέρτερος ‘better, stronger’. The Odyssey translates πολὺ φέρτατος ‘by far the best’; here ‘best’ means best in strength (he could drive them out). The Greek names no group; ‘of us’ in the translation is supplied from the context, the gods who would be driven out. ὃ γάρ is ‘for he’.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σὺ τὸν ἐπέεσσι καθάπτεσθαι μαλακοῖσιν·
sentences.tr: alla sy ton epeessi kathaptesthai malakoisin·
sentences.l: But you, accost him with soft words;
sentences.i: But you, address him directly with soft words;
sentences.n: καθάπτεσθαι is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘do you accost’. καθάπτομαι is ‘fasten upon, address directly’, with the accusative τόν ‘him’ (the article as a pronoun) and the dative ἐπέεσσι ‘with words’; μαλακοῖσιν ‘soft’ is the epic dative plural. The Odyssey has the same pair, καθαπτόμενος … μαλακοῖσι (10.70).

sentences.t: αὐτίκ’ ἔπειθ’ ἵλαος Ὀλύμπιος ἔσσεται ἡμῖν.
sentences.tr: autik’ epeith’ hilaos Olympios essetai hēmin.
sentences.l: at once then gracious the Olympian will be to us.”
sentences.i: and at once the Olympian will be gracious to us.”
sentences.n: αὐτίκ’ ἔπειτα ‘at once, then’ gives the result: if she speaks softly, he will relent. ἵλαος ‘gracious, kindly’ is the epic form of ἵλεως, the adjective that goes with ἱλάσκομαι ‘appease’ (ἱλασσάμενοι at 100). Ὀλύμπιος is Zeus again. Hephaestus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη καὶ ἀναΐξας δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον
μητρὶ φίλῃ ἐν χειρὶ τίθει καί μιν προσέειπε·
sentences.tr:
hōs ar’ ephē kai anaïxas depas amphikypellon
mētri philēi en cheiri tithei kai min proseeipe·
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and having sprung up, a double cup
in his dear mother’s hand he put, and addressed her:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sprang up and put the double cup in his dear mother’s hand, and said to her:
sentences.n: δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is ‘double cup’, and the ancients disagreed whether the cup was double or had a handle on each side, so the word is not quite clear. ἀναΐξας is the aorist participle of ἀναΐσσω ‘spring up’. τίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι ‘put, place’, with ἐν χειρί ‘in her hand’ and μητρὶ φίλῃ ‘to his dear mother’; μιν ‘her’ goes with προσέειπε ‘said to’.

sentences.t: τέτλαθι μῆτερ ἐμή, καὶ ἀνάσχεο κηδομένη περ,
sentences.tr: tetlathi mēter emē, kai anascheo kēdomenē per,
sentences.l: “Endure, my mother, and hold out, grieved though you are,
sentences.i: “Endure it, my mother, and bear up, worried as you are,
sentences.n: τέτλαθι is the perfect imperative of τλάω ‘endure’ (the Odyssey’s ‘Endure now, heart’), with μῆτερ ἐμή ‘my mother’. ἀνάσχεο is the aorist imperative middle of ἀνέχομαι ‘hold out, bear up’. κηδομένη περ ‘though troubled’ is a participle of κήδομαι, which means ‘care for’ at 196 and here ‘be distressed’; περ is ‘though’.

sentences.t:
μή σε φίλην περ ἐοῦσαν ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδωμαι
θεινομένην, τότε δ’ οὔ τι δυνήσομαι ἀχνύμενός περ
χραισμεῖν·
sentences.tr:
mē se philēn per eousan en ophthalmoisin idōmai
theinomenēn, tote d’ ou ti dynēsomai achnymenos per
chraismein·
sentences.i: lest I see you, dear as you are, being struck before my eyes, and then, grieving as I am, I shall be unable to help;
sentences.n: μή … ἴδωμαι is a fear clause, ‘lest I see’, with σε … θεινομένην ‘you being struck’ (the present passive participle of θείνω ‘strike’); φίλην περ ἐοῦσαν is ‘dear though you are’. ἐν ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is literally ‘in the eyes’. The main clause is τότε … οὔ τι δυνήσομαι … χραισμεῖν ‘then I shall not be able to help’, with ἀχνύμενός περ ‘grieving though I am’ (as at 241); χραισμεῖν is the aorist infinitive of χραισμέω, the verb of 566.

sentences.t: ἀργαλέος γὰρ Ὀλύμπιος ἀντιφέρεσθαι·
sentences.tr: argaleos gar Olympios antipheresthai·
sentences.l: for hard is the Olympian to oppose;
sentences.i: for the Olympian is hard to stand against;
sentences.n: ἀργαλέος ‘hard, painful’ takes the infinitive ἀντιφέρεσθαι, the middle of ἀντιφέρω ‘bring oneself against, resist’: ‘hard to resist’. Ὀλύμπιος alone is Zeus, as at 583.

sentences.t:
ἤδη γάρ με καὶ ἄλλοτ’ ἀλεξέμεναι μεμαῶτα
ῥῖψε ποδὸς τεταγὼν ἀπὸ βηλοῦ θεσπεσίοιο,
sentences.tr:
ēdē gar me kai allot’ alexemenai memaōta
rhipse podos tetagōn apo bēlou thespesioio,
sentences.l:
For already me once before, eager to defend,
he flung, seizing me by the foot, from the wondrous threshold,
sentences.i: For once before, when I was eager to defend you, he seized me by the foot and flung me from the wondrous threshold,
sentences.n: ἤδη γὰρ … καὶ ἄλλοτε is ‘for already once before’, the precedent. ἀλεξέμεναι is the infinitive of ἀλέξω ‘ward off, defend’, with μεμαῶτα ‘eager’ (the perfect participle of μέμαα) agreeing with με; the Greek gives no object, and in his mouth it is Hera, so the English supplies ‘you’. ῥῖψε is the aorist of ῥίπτω ‘fling’, and ποδὸς τεταγών ‘having seized by the foot’ (an old aorist participle meaning ‘seize’, with the genitive for the part held). ἀπὸ βηλοῦ θεσπεσίοιο is ‘from the wondrous threshold’: βηλός is the threshold of the gods’ house, and θεσπέσιος is the Odyssey’s ‘wondrous’.

sentences.t:
πᾶν δ’ ἦμαρ φερόμην, ἅμα δ’ ἠελίῳ καταδύντι
κάππεσον ἐν Λήμνῳ, ὀλίγος δ’ ἔτι θυμὸς ἐνῆεν·
sentences.tr:
pan d’ ēmar pheromēn, hama d’ ēeliōi katadynti
kappeson en Lēmnōi, oligos d’ eti thymos enēen·
sentences.l:
all day long I was carried, and with the setting sun
I fell on Lemnos, and little life was still in me;
sentences.i: I was carried all day long, and as the sun went down I fell on Lemnos, with little life still in me;
sentences.n: πᾶν δ’ ἦμαρ ‘the whole day’ is an accusative of duration, and φερόμην the imperfect passive of φέρω, ‘was carried’. ἅμα ἠελίῳ καταδύντι is ‘with the sun setting’ (the aorist participle of καταδύω in the dative). κάππεσον is the aorist of καταπίπτω ‘fall down’, the κατά having become κάπ- before π. Λῆμνος is the island of Lemnos in the north Aegean. ὀλίγος … θυμός is ‘little life’: θυμός is the life-breath that was almost gone; ἐνῆεν is the epic imperfect of ἔνειμι ‘was in’.

sentences.t: ἔνθά με Σίντιες ἄνδρες ἄφαρ κομίσαντο πεσόντα.
sentences.tr: entha me Sinties andres aphar komisanto pesonta.
sentences.l: There the Sintian men at once took care of me when I had fallen.”
sentences.i: There the Sintian men at once took care of me, fallen as I was.”
sentences.n: The Sintians are a people of Lemnos; the Odyssey names them as the island’s inhabitants (8.294). κομίσαντο is the aorist middle of κομίζω ‘take care of, receive and tend’; ἄφαρ ‘at once’; πεσόντα ‘fallen’ is the aorist participle agreeing with με, ‘me who had fallen’. Hephaestus’ speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μείδησεν δὲ θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη,
μειδήσασα δὲ παιδὸς ἐδέξατο χειρὶ κύπελλον·
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, meidēsen de thea leukōlenos Hērē,
meidēsasa de paidos edexato cheiri kypellon·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and smiled the goddess, white-armed Hera,
and smiling she received from her son, by hand, the cup;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the goddess, white-armed Hera, smiled, and with a smile took the cup from her son’s hand;
sentences.n: μείδησεν … μειδήσασα is ‘smiled … smiling’, the aorist of μειδάω first as a finite verb and then as a participle; the smile marks the end of the quarrel. ἐδέξατο is the aorist of δέχομαι ‘take, receive’. The Greek puts παιδός ‘of her son’ (the genitive of the one she takes from) and χειρί ‘by hand’ (a dative) side by side and does not say whose hand; the English reads them together as ‘from her son’s hand’, the usual sense, as he holds out the cup and she takes it. κύπελλον ‘cup’ is the δέπας of 584.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ τοῖς ἄλλοισι θεοῖς ἐνδέξια πᾶσιν
οἰνοχόει γλυκὺ νέκταρ ἀπὸ κρητῆρος ἀφύσσων·
sentences.tr:
autar ho tois alloisi theois endexia pasin
oinochoei glyky nektar apo krētēros aphyssōn·
sentences.l:
but he to the other gods, all of them, towards the right
poured sweet nectar, from the mixing-bowl drawing it;
sentences.i: and he poured sweet nectar for all the other gods in turn, going round to the right, drawing it from the mixing-bowl;
sentences.n: Hephaestus takes over the cup-bearer’s task. αὐτὰρ ὅ is ‘but he’ (the article as a pronoun); τοῖς ἄλλοισι θεοῖς … πᾶσιν is ‘to all the other gods’. ἐνδέξια ‘towards the right’ is the direction of the pouring round the company, as at Odyssey 17.365. οἰνοχόει is the imperfect of οἰνοχοέω ‘pour wine’ (here of nectar), and ἀφύσσων the participle of ἀφύσσω ‘draw up’ (compare 171), with ἀπὸ κρητῆρος ‘from the mixing-bowl’, where the drink was mixed. Nectar is the gods’ drink, as ambrosia is their food.

sentences.t:
ἄσβεστος δ’ ἄρ’ ἐνῶρτο γέλως μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν
ὡς ἴδον Ἥφαιστον διὰ δώματα ποιπνύοντα.
sentences.tr:
asbestos d’ ar’ enōrto gelōs makaressi theoisin
hōs idon Hēphaiston dia dōmata poipnyonta.
sentences.l:
and unquenchable laughter arose among the blessed gods
when they saw Hephaestus bustling through the halls.
sentences.i: and laughter that would never go out rose among the blessed gods when they saw Hephaestus bustling through the halls.
sentences.n: The first line is the Odyssey’s (8.326), said there of the gods laughing at Ares and Aphrodite in the net. ἄσβεστος ‘unquenchable’ (ἀ- + σβέννυμι ‘quench’) is the word the Odyssey’s English renders ‘that would never go out’; ἐνῶρτο is the aorist of ἐνόρνυμι ‘arise in’; μακάρεσσι θεοῖσιν ‘among the blessed gods’. They laugh at the lame smith playing cup-bearer. ἴδον ‘saw’ is the aorist of ὁράω with the augment lost, and ποιπνύοντα ‘bustling’ is the participle of ποιπνύω, the Odyssey’s verb for hurried service.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε μὲν πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
δαίνυντ’, οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης,
sentences.tr:
hōs tote men propan ēmar es ēelion katadynta
dainynt’, oude ti thymos edeueto daitos eïsēs,
sentences.l:
So then for the whole day, until the sun going down,
they feasted, and not at all did the heart lack the equal feast,
sentences.i: So for that whole day, until the sun went down, they feasted, and their hearts went short of nothing in the equally shared feast,
sentences.n: The first line is the Odyssey’s (9.161); the second is the line that ends the feast at 468. ὣς τότε μέν ‘so then, for that time’ takes πρόπαν ἦμαρ ‘the whole day’ as an accusative of duration, ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα ‘until the sun going down’. δαίνυντ’ is δαίνυντο ‘they feasted’. οὐδέ τι θυμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης is ‘not at all did the heart lack the equal feast’: ἐδεύετο is the imperfect of δεύομαι ‘lack’, which takes the genitive, and δαιτὸς ἐΐσης is the feast shared out in equal portions. The genitives of the next unit depend on the same verb.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν φόρμιγγος περικαλλέος ἣν ἔχ’ Ἀπόλλων,
Μουσάων θ’ αἳ ἄειδον ἀμειβόμεναι ὀπὶ καλῇ.
sentences.tr:
ou men phormingos perikalleos hēn ech’ Apollōn,
Mousaōn th’ hai aeidon ameibomenai opi kalēi.
sentences.l:
nor yet of the very beautiful lyre which Apollo held,
and of the Muses, who sang, answering one another with a beautiful voice.
sentences.i: nor did they lack the very beautiful lyre that Apollo held, or the Muses, who sang, answering one another in beautiful voice.
sentences.n: The genitives φόρμιγγος and Μουσάων depend on ἐδεύετο of 602: ‘nor [did the heart lack] the lyre … or the Muses’. οὐ μέν is ‘nor yet’. φόρμιγξ is the lyre and περικαλλέος ‘very beautiful’; ἔχ’ is ἔχε, the imperfect, ‘held’. Μουσάων is the epic genitive plural of Μοῦσα (Attic Μουσῶν). ἄειδον ‘sang’ is the imperfect of ἀείδω, the verb of the poem’s first word; ἀμειβόμεναι ‘answering one another, taking turns’; ὀπὶ καλῇ ‘with a beautiful voice’ (ὄψ, ὀπός ‘voice’).

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ κατέδυ λαμπρὸν φάος ἠελίοιο,
οἳ μὲν κακκείοντες ἔβαν οἶκον δὲ ἕκαστος,
sentences.tr:
autar epei katedy lampron phaos ēelioio,
hoi men kakkeiontes eban oikon de hekastos,
sentences.l:
But when the bright light of the sun had gone down,
they, to lie down going, went home, each one,
sentences.i: But when the bright light of the sun had gone down, they went off home to bed, each of them,
sentences.n: κατέδυ ‘went down’ is the aorist of καταδύω (as at 475), and λαμπρὸν φάος ἠελίοιο ‘the bright light of the sun’ is a poetic way of saying ‘sunset’. οἳ μέν ‘they for their part’ (the gods). κακκείοντες is the desiderative participle of κατακείω ‘wish to lie down’, the κατά assimilated to κακ- before κ, as in the Odyssey’s formula κακκείοντες ἔβαν οἶκόνδε ἕκαστος; here the edition prints οἶκον δέ as two words, ‘homewards’. ἔβαν is the aorist ἔβησαν ‘went’.

sentences.t:
ἧχι ἑκάστῳ δῶμα περικλυτὸς ἀμφιγυήεις
Ἥφαιστος ποίησεν ἰδυίῃσι πραπίδεσσι·
sentences.tr:
hēchi hekastōi dōma periklytos amphigyēeis
Hēphaistos poiēsen iduiēisi prapidessi·
sentences.l:
where for each a house the very-famous both-limbed one,
Hephaestus, had made with knowing wits;
sentences.i: to the place where the very famous both-limbed god, Hephaestus, had made each a house with his skilled wits;
sentences.n: ἧχι ‘where’ (epic), with ἑκάστῳ ‘for each’: every god has a house on Olympus built by Hephaestus. ἀμφιγυήεις is of unknown meaning (the ancients said ‘lame in both legs’ or ‘strong in both arms’), so ‘both-limbed’ is only the literal form, ἀμφί ‘on both sides’ + γυῖον ‘limb’; with περικλυτός ‘very famous’ it is the stock formula for Hephaestus. ἰδυίῃσι πραπίδεσσι ‘with knowing wits’ (ἰδυῖα is the perfect participle of οἶδα, and πραπίδες the mind) is the Odyssey’s phrase for his craft (7.92).

sentences.t:
Ζεὺς δὲ πρὸς ὃν λέχος ἤϊ’ Ὀλύμπιος ἀστεροπητής,
ἔνθα πάρος κοιμᾶθ’ ὅτε μιν γλυκὺς ὕπνος ἱκάνοι·
sentences.tr:
Zeus de pros hon lechos ēï’ Olympios asteropētēs,
entha paros koimath’ hote min glykys hypnos hikanoi·
sentences.l:
and Zeus to his own bed went, the Olympian, the lightning-flasher,
where before he used to sleep, whenever sweet sleep might come on him;
sentences.i: Zeus, the Olympian who flashes lightning, went to his own bed, where he used to sleep whenever sweet sleep came upon him;
sentences.n: ὃν λέχος is ‘his own bed’ (ὅς, the possessive, not the relative). ἤϊ’ is ἤϊε, the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, its last vowel elided. Ὀλύμπιος ἀστεροπητής is the pair of 580. The second line is the Odyssey’s, said there of Telemachus going to his room (19.49): ἔνθα πάρος κοιμᾶθ’ is ‘where before he used to sleep’ (κοιμᾶτο, the imperfect middle of κοιμάω), and ὅτε … ἱκάνοι, ὅτε with the optative of ἱκάνω ‘come upon’, is ‘whenever sweet sleep came upon him’.

sentences.t: ἔνθα καθεῦδ’ ἀναβάς, παρὰ δὲ χρυσόθρονος Ἥρη.
sentences.tr: entha katheud’ anabas, para de chrysothronos Hērē.
sentences.l: there he slept, having mounted, and beside him golden-throned Hera.
sentences.i: There he went up and slept, and beside him slept golden-throned Hera.
sentences.n: καθεῦδ’ is the imperfect of καθεύδω ‘sleep’, with ἀναβάς ‘having gone up’ (aorist participle of ἀναβαίνω): he climbs onto the high bed. The verb of the second half is understood, ‘beside him [slept] Hera’; παρά ‘beside’ is an adverb here. χρυσόθρονος is Hera’s epithet, ‘golden-throned’, as the Odyssey gives it to Dawn and Artemis; the second part may instead come from θρόνα ‘embroidered flowers’, an old alternative reading. This is the last line of Book 1.
